group.passage: Even Winnie the Pooh might be surprised at this: not all bees buzz around a hive, make honey, or serve a queen. In fact, the hive-oriented social bees are the exception in the bee world. Over 90% of the world’s bee species lead solitary lives instead. Solitary bees typically live for a year, but their active adult stage lasts only a few weeks. Most of their life is spent developing inside their nests. In spring, they emerge and mate. Shortly after mating, males die, while females begin nesting, usually in natural tunnels or artificial ones in beehouses. Inside the nest, the female constructs several separate cells divided by mud, each holding a single egg and supplied with a ball of pollen and nectar as food. To protect her young, she also lines the cells with waxy secretions, leaves, or petals. With just weeks to work, she races against time to complete nesting before dying. The larvae then feed on the stored food in their individual chambers throughout winter, emerging the following spring as adults to begin the cycle anew. Solitary bees play a vital role in the ecosystem. Despite receiving less attention than social bees, they are far more effective pollinators—oddly because they are clumsier at collecting pollen. Unlike honeybees that carry pollen moistened with nectar in leg baskets, solitary bees transport dry, loose pollen on specialized underbelly hairs. As they land on flowers, the dry pollen they carry falls off more easily than moist pollen. It’s great news for pollination, but it means they must work harder to gather enough pollen for their own needs. Solitary bees are also known for their gentle disposition. Since they don’t have a hive or a store of honey to defend, they hardly ever show the hostility observed in social bees and they rarely sting. This, in turn, makes them a welcome presence in our gardens. Due to their wild nature, solitary bees are hard to protect. Still, we can start by planting bee-friendly flowers, reducing pesticide use, and providing artificial beehouses made of wood or bamboo. So why not stay calm next time you see a bee hovering nearby? It probably has more important things to do than sting you.

figures.label: 第1題選項(A)
figures.caption: 第1題選項(A)：管狀巢穴，每室多顆卵
figures.description: 黑白線條插圖：一條橫放的長管狀巢穴（左端圓弧封閉、右端開口），內部以數道弧形泥牆隔成一格一格的小室。最內側（左端）小室裡有一隻捲曲的幼蟲趴在一團花粉上；其餘小室各有一團花粉，每團花粉上有兩三顆小橢圓形的卵（不只一顆）；靠開口的最右側小室有一隻成蜂，頭朝向開口。

figures.label: 第1題選項(B)
figures.caption: 第1題選項(B)：管狀巢穴，每室一顆卵
figures.description: 黑白線條插圖：一條橫放的長管狀巢穴（左端開口、右端圓弧封閉），內部以數道弧形泥牆隔成五個獨立小室，每個小室各有一團花粉（花粉與花蜜做成的食物球），每團花粉上只有一顆卵；靠開口的最左側有一隻成蜂，頭朝向開口。

figures.label: 第1題選項(C)
figures.caption: 第1題選項(C)：六角形蜂巢
figures.description: 黑白線條插圖：由許多六角形巢室組成的蜂巢片（群居蜜蜂的蜂巢），左側停著一隻蜜蜂；巢室中分別有放在花粉上的卵、捲曲的幼蟲、直立的蛹，也有空的巢室。

figures.label: 第1題選項(D)
figures.caption: 第1題選項(D)：地底巢穴
figures.description: 黑白線條插圖：地底巢穴剖面圖。地表長著草，右上方有一條通往地下的隧道入口，一隻蜂正在入口處；地下是一個橢圓形的大巢室，內部分成上下三層，每層都並排放著好幾團花粉、卵與幼蟲（同一層有多顆卵，並非一室一卵）。

questions.stem: According to the passage, which picture best describes the inside of a solitary bee nest?

options.A: ［圖］長條管狀巢穴（左端封閉、右端開口），以泥牆隔成數個小室；最內側小室有一隻幼蟲在花粉團上，其餘小室的花粉團上各有兩三顆卵；開口處有一隻成蜂頭朝外。
options.B: ［圖］長條管狀巢穴（左端開口、右端封閉），以泥牆隔成五個獨立小室，每個小室各有一團花粉，上面只有一顆卵；開口處有一隻成蜂頭朝外。
options.C: ［圖］六角形蜂巢片上停著一隻蜜蜂，巢室中有卵、捲曲的幼蟲與蛹，也有空巢室。
options.D: ［圖］地底巢穴剖面：地面長草，一隻蜂在右上方的隧道入口；地下橢圓形大巢室分成上下三層，每層並排放著好幾團花粉、卵與幼蟲。

questions.stem: What does “This” in the third paragraph refer to?

options.A: Solitary bees don’t have a sting.
options.C: Solitary bees are more effective pollinators.

questions.stem: How does the author conclude the passage in the last paragraph?
What can be inferred from the passage?

options.A: The faster female solitary bees complete nesting, the better their larvae will develop.
options.B: Male solitary bees emerge earlier than females to collect leaves and petals for nesting.
options.C: Solitary bees need to make more flower visits to collect as much pollen as honeybees.
options.D: Most bees in our gardens are social bees, while solitary bees are mostly found in the wild.
